newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico vows to renew drug cooperation with Colombia.
newsitem.headline: Mexico vows to renew drug cooperation with Colombia.

text.p: Mexico on Tuesday said it would send a top-level anti-drugs envoy to Colombia after the Colombians complained they did not have a Mexican point person to coordinate with in the war on drugs.

The rumblings by Colombia's chief anti-drugs warrior coincided with statements by a top U.S. drug official that Mexican traffickers were eclipsing their Colombian counterparts in domination of the U.S. drugs market.
Colombia is the world's largest producer of cocaine, much of which passes through Mexico on its way to the United States.

Despite high-profile summits in the past decade to promote international anti-drug cooperation, Mexico admitted on Tuesday that it had no designated "interlocutor" to cooperate with Colombia on drug investigations.

Mariano Herran Salvatti, chief of Mexico's new Special Prosecutor's Office for Crimes against Health, said in a live radio interview on Tuesday that Mexico would send an envoy to Colombia, but it had not been decided whether that person would be a diplomat or a cop.
"The Mexican government will review the possibility of having a Mexican representative in Colombia as we have in other countries," Herran told Radio Red.
Colombia's Gen. Rosso Jose Serrano, chief of the National Police, told Radio Red on Monday that it had been several months since Colombia has known who to share information with in Mexico.

The breakdown stemmed from a Mexican restructuring of its anti-drug forces amid allegations of high-level corruption. The most serious breach was revealed in February, when anti-drugs chief Gen. Jesus Gutierrez Rebollo was arrested on charges that he was part of the payroll of Mexico's leading drug baron.

"I say this with a little bit of sadness that I don't have an interlocutor in Mexico," Serrano said Monday. "As a result, we sit on information because we don't know who to send it to. So I think we have to call this to someone's attention."

Herran said it would be up to the newly designated Mexican ambassador to determine whether Mexico would send an attache to work out of the embassy or an agent of the Attorney General's Office (PGR) who would work directly with Colombian police.
The Mexican Senate on Monday confirmed the appointment of Andres Valencia as ambassador to Colombia, but a foreign ministry spokeswoman told Reuters it was unknown when he would take up his new post.
Both Mexico's Salvatti and Colombia's Serrano said cooperation between the two countries is vital.
On Monday, the chief of the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) underscored the point.
"These organised syndicates whose leadership is based in Mexico ... are moving closer to eclipsing the Colombians and controlling the U.S. drug market," Thomas Constantine said.
